label: Survival Mandarin
blurb: The phrases you need in your first weeks — by ear and meaning, no reading required.
blurbZh: 剛到台灣前幾週最需要的那些話。只靠聽和意思，不需要認字。

questions.q: Someone you have just met says 你好. They are —
questions.why: 你好 (nǐ hǎo) is the all-purpose hello. Safe with anyone, any time of day.

questions.q: A colleague hands you a coffee. You say —
questions.why: 謝謝 (xièxie) is thank you, and it is the single most useful word on this list. Use it freely — it is never too much.

questions.q: You step on someone's foot in the corridor. You say —
questions.why: 對不起 (duìbùqǐ) is a real apology — you did something. For the lighter "excuse me" when squeezing past, 不好意思 is the usual choice.

questions.q: You are leaving the office at the end of the day. You say —
questions.why: 再見 (zàijiàn) is goodbye. Colleagues often say 掰掰 (bāibāi) too — the same word English lent them.

questions.q: Walking into the office at 7:40 a.m., you greet colleagues with —
questions.why: 早安 (zǎo'ān) is good morning. Many people shorten it to just 早 (zǎo) — one syllable, and completely normal.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 老師 (lǎoshī) is teacher, and it is also how people will address you — often with your surname in front, or on its own.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 校長 (xiàozhǎng) is the principal. You will hear this in every staff meeting.

questions.q: You did not understand what was just said. You say —
questions.why: 我不懂 (wǒ bù dǒng) — I don't understand. Nobody minds hearing it; what causes trouble is nodding when you did not follow.

questions.q: You want someone to repeat what they said. You say —
opts: 請再說一次 (qǐng zài shuō yí cì)
我先走了 (wǒ xiān zǒu le)
questions.why: 請再說一次 (qǐng zài shuō yí cì) — please say it once more. Pair it with 慢一點 (màn yìdiǎn), "a bit slower", and you can get through most conversations.

questions.q: Someone is speaking too fast for you. You ask for —
questions.why: 慢一點 (màn yìdiǎn) — a bit slower. More useful than asking for English, because it keeps you in the conversation.

questions.q: Listen. What are they asking about?
questions.why: 廁所 (cèsuǒ) is the toilet. 廁所在哪裡 (cèsuǒ zài nǎlǐ) — where is the toilet — is worth memorizing whole.

questions.q: At a food stall you want to know the price. You ask —
questions.why: 多少錢 (duōshǎo qián) — how much. Expect the answer as a number you may not catch; a calculator or their fingers usually follows.

questions.q: You cannot name the dish, so you point at it and say —
questions.why: 這個 (zhège) — this one. Point and say it, and you can order anything without knowing a single food word.

questions.q: You are vegetarian and want to say so before ordering. You say —
questions.why: 我吃素 (wǒ chīsù) — I'm vegetarian. Widely understood in Taiwan, where 素食 is common and well catered for.

questions.q: You want your food without chili. You say —
questions.why: 不要辣 (bú yào là) — no chili. The same pattern works for anything: 不要 plus the thing you do not want.

questions.q: Someone proposes a time to meet and you agree. The shortest reply is —
questions.why: 好 (hǎo) on its own means fine / OK / agreed. One syllable, and it carries an enormous amount of daily conversation.

questions.q: Someone apologizes for a small mistake. You reassure them with —
questions.why: 沒關係 (méi guānxi) — it doesn't matter, no harm done. The standard reply to an apology.

questions.q: Someone thanks you. You reply —
questions.why: 不客氣 (bú kèqi) — you're welcome. Note the tone: 不 rises here, bú, because 客 falls.

questions.q: Listen. What is starting?
questions.why: 上課 (shàngkè) — class begins. Its opposite, 下課 (xiàkè), is the bell you will learn fastest.

questions.q: Listen. What has just happened?
questions.why: 下課 (xiàkè) — class is over. Ten minutes between periods, and the corridor will tell you before the word does.

questions.q: You need to squeeze past someone in a narrow corridor. You say —
questions.why: 不好意思 (bù hǎoyìsi) is the everyday excuse-me — passing someone, interrupting, asking a small favor. Lighter than 對不起.

questions.q: You are about to ask a stranger for directions. You open with —
questions.why: 請問 (qǐngwèn) — may I ask. It signals a question is coming and makes it polite before you have said anything else.

questions.q: You are looking for a place and want to ask where it is. You use —
questions.why: 在哪裡 (zài nǎlǐ) — where is it. Put the place in front: 廁所在哪裡, 辦公室在哪裡.

questions.q: Listen. What is happening?
questions.why: 開會 (kāihuì) — to have a meeting. If you hear it with a time attached, that time is probably yours too.
